translations.text: In the days when the judges ruled, a famine came upon the land. A man from Bethlehem in Judah went to live in the countryside of Moab, with his wife and his two sons.

The man's name was Elimelech, his wife's name was Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went to the countryside of Moab and stayed there.
Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons.
They married Moabite women. The name of one was Orpah, and the name of the other was Ruth. They lived there for about ten years.
Both Mahlon and Chilion died there, and the woman was left alone, without her husband or her sons.
She and her two daughters-in-law arose and returned from the countryside of Moab, because they had heard that God had attended to his people by giving them bread.
She left the place where she had been living, with her two daughters-in-law, and they set out on the road to return to the land of Judah.
Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go, each of you, back to your father's house. May the Lord show you kindness, as you have shown kindness to the dead and to me."
"May the Lord grant that each of you find rest in the house of her husband." Then she kissed them, and they raised their voices and wept.
They said to her, "No, we will return with you to your people."
Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Could I still have sons in my womb who would become your husbands?"
"Turn back, my daughters, and go, for I have grown old and cannot marry a man. Even if I were to say that there was still hope for me, and I were to marry a man and bear sons,"

"would you wait for them until they grew up? Would you hold yourselves back for them and not marry? No, my daughters, for I am more embittered than you, because the Lord's hand has gone out against me."
They raised their voices again and wept. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and returned to her people, but Ruth followed her.
Naomi said to Ruth, “Look, your sister-in-law has returned to her people and to her gods. You too should return after your sister-in-law.”
Ruth said, "May I never leave you and turn back from you. Where you go, I will go, and where you rest, I will rest. Your people will be my people, and your God my God."
"Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the Lord do so to me, and more besides, if anything but death separates me from you."
When Naomi saw that she was determined to go with her, she stopped speaking to her about it.
The two of them went on until they reached Bethlehem. When they arrived in Bethlehem, the whole city was stirred because of her, and they said, “Is this Naomi?”
She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi, but call me Bitter, for the Almighty has made me very bitter."
"I went away full, and the Lord has brought me back empty. Why, then, do you call me Naomi, when the Lord has brought me low and the Almighty has afflicted me?"
Naomi returned, with Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, coming with her from the countryside of Moab. They came to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
There was a man acquainted with Naomi's husband, a powerful man from Elimelech's family, whose name was Boaz. He gave Naomi a house to live in during her widowhood.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the field and glean ears of grain behind someone in whose eyes I find favor." She said to her, "Go, my daughter."
She went out and gleaned ears of grain in the field behind the reapers. By chance she came to the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, a relative of Elimelech.
Boaz came from Bethlehem and said to his reapers, "The Lord be with you." They said to him, "May the Lord bless you."
Boaz said to his young man who was in charge of the reapers, "Whose girl is that?"
The young man in charge of the reapers answered, “She is the Moabite girl who returned with Naomi from the country of Moab.”

“She said, ‘Please let me glean and gather ears of grain among the sheaves behind the reapers.’ She came and has remained from morning until now, without stopping or resting even a little in the fields.”
Boaz said to Ruth, “Do you hear, my daughter? Do not go elsewhere to glean ears of grain in other fields, and do not leave this place at all. Stay here with my young women.”

“Keep your eyes on the fields where they are reaping, and follow them. Have I not ordered my young men not to approach you? If you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink from the water the young men draw.”
She fell on her face and bowed low to the ground, saying, “Why have I found favor in your eyes, so that you take notice of me, though I am a foreign woman?”

Boaz answered her, “I have been fully told everything you have done for your mother-in-law since your husband’s death, and how you left your father, your mother, and the land of your birth, and came to a people you had not known before.”
May the Lord repay you for your work, and may your reward be full from the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.
She said, “I have found favor in your eyes, my lord, because you have comforted me and spoken to the heart of your servant, and I will be like one of your servant women.”

Boaz said to her, “Now is a good time. Come here, eat some bread, and dip your piece in the vinegar.” Ruth sat beside the reapers, and Boaz mixed some roasted grain flour for her. She ate, was satisfied, and left some over.
She got up to glean ears of grain, and Boaz instructed his young men, saying, “Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not put her to shame.”
But also deliberately take some out and throw it down before her from the mixed [?]. Leave her alone, and let her eat and glean ears of grain, and do not bother her.
She gleaned in the field until evening and beat out what she had gleaned. It amounted to one measure of barley.
She took it and went into the town. When her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned, Ruth brought out and gave her what she had left over after eating her fill.

Her mother-in-law said to her, “Where did you gather grain today, and where were you? Blessed be the one who took notice of you.” Ruth told her mother-in-law where she had been and gave the name of the man with whom she had been that day, saying, “It is Boaz.”

Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “May he be blessed by the Lord, for he has not withheld his kindness from the living or the dead.” Naomi also said to her, “The man is closely related to us; he is one of our close relatives.”
Ruth said to her mother-in-law, “Indeed, he told me, ‘Stay with my young women until they finish all my harvesting.’”
Naomi said to Ruth, her daughter-in-law, “It is good, my daughter, that you have been with his young women, so that no one encounters you in another field.”
Ruth stayed with Boaz’s young women to glean ears of grain until the barley harvest and the wheat harvest were finished, and she lived with her mother-in-law.
Naomi, her mother-in-law, said to her, “Daughter, I will seek a place of rest for you, so that things may go well for you.”
“Now, is not Boaz our relative, whose young women you were with? Look, he is winnowing barley at the threshing floor tonight.”
“Wash yourself, anoint yourself, put on your clothes, and go up to the threshing floor. Do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking.”
“When he goes to sleep, take note of the place where he lies down. Then go, uncover the place at his feet, and lie down. He will tell you what you are to do.”
Ruth said to her, “I will do everything you tell me.”
She went down to the threshing floor and did everything just as her mother-in-law had instructed her.
Boaz ate and drank, and his heart was cheerful. He went and lay down beside the heap of grain. She came quietly, uncovered the place at his feet, and lay down.
At midnight the man was startled and became agitated, and there was a woman lying at his feet.
He said, “Who are you?” She said, “I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your cloak over your servant, for you are a kinsman-redeemer.”
Boaz said, “May you be blessed by the Lord God, my daughter, for you have shown greater kindness now than before, because you did not go after young men, whether poor or of high standing.”
And now, my daughter, do not be afraid. I will do for you everything you ask of me, for the whole community of my people knows that you are a woman of worth.
Indeed, I am your kinsman-redeemer, but there is another kinsman-redeemer who is more closely related than I am.
Stay here tonight, and in the morning, if your kinsman will redeem you, that is good. But if he is unwilling to redeem you, I will redeem you, as the Lord lives. Lie down here until morning.
She lay at his feet until morning, and the woman rose before anyone could recognize his companion. Boaz said, “Let no one know that a woman came to me at the threshing floor.”
“Bring the cloak you are wearing and hold it here.” She held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then he went into the city.
Ruth went to her mother-in-law, who said, “How is it, my daughter?” She told her everything the man had done for her.
She said to her, “He gave me these six measures of barley and said, ‘Do not go empty-handed to your mother-in-law.’”
She said, “Stay here until it becomes clear to us that the matter will not fail, for the man will not rest until he settles the matter this very day.”

Boaz went up to the gate and sat there. And behold, the kinsman-redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken was passing by him. Boaz said to him, “Come over and sit here a little while, and stay.” He came over and sat down.
Boaz took ten men from among the elders of the city and said, “Sit here.” And they sat down.
Boaz said to the kinsman-redeemer, “Naomi, who has returned from the country of Moab, is selling the portion of land belonging to our brother Elimelech.

I thought I would tell you about it. Now buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people. If you will redeem it, redeem it; but if you will not redeem it, tell me so that I may know, for there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I am the next kinsman-redeemer after you.”
Boaz said, “On the day you acquire the field from Naomi and from Ruth the Moabite, the dead man's wife, you must also acquire her and preserve the dead man's name in his inheritance.”
The kinsman-redeemer said to Boaz, “I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I ruin my own inheritance. Exercise my right of redemption for yourself, for I cannot redeem it.”

This was formerly the custom in Israel concerning redemption and purchase: to confirm any transaction, a man took off his sandal and gave it to his companion, who was to exercise his right of redemption. This served as testimony in Israel.
The kinsman-redeemer said to Boaz, “Acquire my right of redemption for yourself.” He took off his sandal and gave it to him.
Boaz said to the elders and to all the people, “You are my witnesses today that I have acquired from Naomi everything belonging to Elimelech and everything belonging to Chilion and Mahlon.

I have also acquired Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon's wife, as my wife, to preserve the dead man's name in his inheritance, so that the dead man's name may not be erased from among his brothers and from the community of his own place. You are witnesses today.”

All the people at the gate answered, “We are witnesses.” And the elders said, “May the Lord make the woman who is entering your house like Rachel and Leah, who together built the house of Israel. May you prosper in Ephrathah and make a name in Bethlehem.
May your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, through that offspring; and may the Lord give you a son by this young woman.”
Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. He went in to her, and the Lord granted her conception, and she bore a son.
The women said to Naomi, “Blessed be the Lord, who has not taken a kinsman-redeemer away from you today, so that your name may be proclaimed in Israel.
He shall restore your life and sustain you in your old age, for your daughter-in-law, who loved you, has borne a son who is better for you than seven sons.”
And Naomi took the child, laid him in her lap, and became his nurse.
And the neighbors gave him a name, saying, “A son has been born to Naomi,” and they named him Obed. He is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
And this is the genealogy of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron.
And Hezron fathered Ram; Ram fathered Amminadab.
Amminadab fathered Nahshon; Nahshon fathered Salmon.
Salmon fathered Boaz; Boaz fathered Obed.
Obed fathered Jesse; Jesse fathered David.
